# Practice track workspace template

A self-contained template for agent-managed workspaces in which **the user practises a tool or technology stack by implementing fully guided plans**. The aim is exposure and practice, not independence through fading guidance: every plan is a small, self-contained project built from complete steps, so the user meets each feature hands-on, remembers that it exists and where it helps, and looks the details up when a real need arises. Working things out without steps is deliberately out of scope; the user does that in separate projects of their own.

A workspace covers one track, such as a game engine or a web stack. It works through a bounded **core** of topic clusters chosen for their value to the user's goal, planned one **arc** (a few plans) at a time, with time estimates checked against the hours actually spent. Topics that complete text steps teach poorly, such as art, modelling or level design, stay out of the plans.

Other templates in the family: `MANUAL_IMPLEMENTATION_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (the user implements; the agent coaches with fading support levels), `AGENTIC_LEARNING_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (the agent implements step by step while the user builds along and learns), `AUTONOMOUS_AGENTIC_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (agents build end to end; the user approves at milestone gates) and `ITERATIVE_HYBRID_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (human-first with agent acceleration; the direction evolves and plans are written just in time).

## How to use this template

Provide this file to the agent (from the canonical repository or a local copy), together with the add-ons the track uses (see *Optional add-ons*), and describe the track: the tool or stack, the goal the practice serves, what the user already knows, and the time available (sessions per week, their usual length and days). For example:

> Read PRACTICE_TRACK_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md and use it to scaffold a practice workspace for <tool or stack>. Goal: <what the practice is for>. I practise <sessions> a week, about <length> each. I already know <…>. Create the roadmap with its first arc and only the first detailed plan.

The example invocation does not need to be stored in generated documentation.

## Template use and updates

- The template is not retained in generated workspaces by default; a provenance note pointing to the canonical source is enough. Keep a retained copy only if the user asks for one. A template is not an automatically active `AGENTS.md` and is never copied verbatim into one.
- Generated workspaces record the canonical template file and the add-ons used as references in `docs/MEMORY.md` and in the generated `AGENTS.md`, once each, never as a local copy. If a recorded path is missing, ask the user for the updated path instead of guessing.
- When a workspace format or process change is agreed during a project, propose the matching template update so other workspaces inherit it. The templates are generated: edits go to the parts in the template repository's `src/` folder (`src/shared/` for rules every template uses, the template's own folder otherwise), then `scripts/build-templates.ps1` rebuilds them.
- The agent applies the process to the actual workspace, following the applicable instruction hierarchy and the user's current directions. The user can override the workflow and role defaults at any time. Preserve already-authorized scope instead of asking for the same permission again.

## Shared working rules

The working agreement states the working role; these rules hold alongside it.

- Records (`ROADMAP.md` states, `MEMORY.md` history, decisions, conventions, the time log) and their compaction are agent-maintained; the user can inspect them at any time.
- Keep replies short and answer first: lead with the answer or verdict, then any issues with their fixes, an explanation only when it is new to the user or changes the next step, and end with `Next:` and the user's action. Leave out bookkeeping (files edited, records updated) unless asked for or blocking. Aim for one line, or under about 150 words. `Next:` points into the plan when the step is there (`Next: 4.3.`); spell the action out only when the plan doesn't cover it, such as a correction, evidence to send or an editor restart. Answer status check-ins ("what's next", "current status") with the current position and next action as pointers; keep steps and values in the plan and repeat them only when asked.
- Git, tool installs, publishing and external communication are user-managed unless explicitly delegated or requested; record a delegation and its boundaries in `MEMORY.md` conventions and `AGENTS.md`. Once source control is set up, individual commit/push operations are not tracked in the records; check the repository state directly when needed.
- Irreversible, destructive, costly or externally visible actions require explicit authorization for that action.
- Preserve existing work; do not reset, clean, move or overwrite unrelated material.
- No sub-agents unless the user or applicable instructions explicitly request them.
- The user can stop and resume at any point: the records must stand alone.

## Working agreement

- **The user implements every plan.** The agent writes the plans with complete steps, explains concepts where a plan first needs them, answers questions, reviews the result at the end of each plan (or when asked), performs authorized verification and maintains the records: the roadmap with its time section and coverage map, the time log, the toolbox and the history.
- Creating or rewriting project code, assets, levels or configuration requires an explicit user request; documentation and non-destructive checks are normal agent work. Setup the user delegates in a plan step (for example enabling an editor bridge in a new project) covers only that step.
- **Plan scope.** Plans cover what complete text steps teach well: work whose result is judged by whether it is right, such as logic, systems, configuration, code, data, tooling and builds. Work judged by eye, ear or feel, or learned better from video, such as art, modelling, animation authoring, level design and sound design, stays out of the plans; plans use template, engine or free assets in its place. An out-of-scope tool appears only in a small, simple step when the alternative is harder to obtain or complicates the plan, and then with complete steps like any other.
- **No fading.** Step detail never shrinks with repetition, and plans never rely on the user remembering an earlier plan (see *Step detail*). There is no skill ledger and no support levels.
- Questions get direct and complete answers; working things out alone is not a goal of this workspace.
- Reviews give finding, location, consequence, suggested correction and a way to verify. The user applies corrections, added as fix steps to the current plan, unless the agent has been asked to edit.

## Bootstrap procedure

1. Inspect existing instructions, files, documentation, implementation and repository state; identify what exists before proposing a structure.
2. Determine whether this is one project or a workspace of independently managed projects; use existing organization and user intent.
3. Extract confirmed requirements from the supplied material; keep proposals, assumptions, open questions and observed facts distinct.
4. Calibrate (see *Bootstrap additions*). Default user profile when nothing else is supplied: comfortable with general programming; no experience with this project's tools, frameworks, engine or conventions. Explain those at first use and skip generic programming lessons. Record only knowledge the user states for this workspace; do not carry it over from elsewhere or invent preferences.
5. Verify what the agent can verify itself (environment, installed tools, filesystem) before authoring plans.
6. Resolve ordinary organizational choices from available context; ask only questions that materially affect scope, correctness or the immediate plan. If requirements are missing, request them without inventing a product or domain; neutral scaffolding may still be prepared.
7. Check which add-ons the project needs (see *Optional add-ons*). Use the ones provided; for a needed add-on that was not provided, name it and ask for it, or proceed without it and state what is missing.
8. Preserve useful existing documents; adapt or link them instead of duplicating conflicting versions.
9. Generate the minimum coherent set: `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/MEMORY.md`, a domain document only when the project has one (several → `docs/design/` with an index), the first detailed plan with its toolbox entries (`docs/toolbox.md`), and the agent-client entry files the user's clients need (see *Resume routine, AGENTS.md and client entry files*). No session files, no separate status, conventions, decisions, references or verification documents.
10. Check consistency of links, states and evidence labels; finish with the audit and handoff (see *Final audit and handoff*).

Scaffolding produces documentation only. Do not create product files, install dependencies, contact external services or initialize source control unless that work is separately requested or already authorized.

## Bootstrap additions

- **Calibration** (bootstrap step 4) records in the `AGENTS.md` user profile what the user already knows, so explanations stay short there (steps stay complete regardless), and what is new, so it is explained at first use. It also records the time budget: sessions per week, their usual length and the days they fall on.
- **Coverage map** (see *Arcs, coverage and time*): list the track's topic clusters, mark the ones the user practised before this workspace, tag each `core` or `later` by its value to the user's goal, and list the out-of-scope topics once with where the user learns them instead. Size the core to the time budget and state the period it is expected to take.
- **Roadmap:** the time section, the first arc with its plans as one-line outcomes, the later core arcs as one-line themes, and the coverage map. Only the first plan is written in detail.
- Verification (bootstrap step 5) exists so plans carry only user actions: check the installed tools and versions and the starter or template content the first plan uses, and note what the later arcs will need that is not yet checked.
- Handoff: report the entry point, the current plan, the next action and the core's time estimate.

## Workspace structure

Preserve established naming and layout when they already provide the same responsibilities; record intentional deviations in `MEMORY.md` conventions.

### Single project

```text
<workspace>/
  README.md                Entry point: purpose, layout, how the workspace works
  AGENTS.md                Agent operating rules, resume routine, role-specific protocol
  CLAUDE.md                Optional client entry file: a pointer to AGENTS.md
  docs/
    ROADMAP.md             Roadmap, plan states, resume pointer; gates and notes as needed
    MEMORY.md              Decisions, conventions, the time log, references, history
    history/YYYY-MM.md     Optional: archived history moved out of MEMORY at compaction
    <domain>.md            Project-specific concept or design document(s), as needed
    design/                Optional, when there are several domain docs: README.md index + one doc per system
    toolbox.md             The toolbox: the glossary of features met so far (what, use it when, built in, nearby, docs)
    tooling-notes.md       Optional: tool recipes and environment reference too long for MEMORY
    tooling/               Optional, when several tools need notes: one file per tool instead of tooling-notes.md
    implementation-plans/
      NN-<name>.md            One current detailed plan; completed plans remain as records
    refs/                  Optional reference library: captures, fetched sets (+ `_sources.md` provenance), generated diagrams
  <delivery-root>/         Implementation lives where the project needs it
```

### Multiple projects

Repeat the `docs/` set per project (for example under `projects/<id>/`), keep the workspace-level `README.md` and `AGENTS.md`, and add a small registry (`PROJECTS.md` or a roadmap section) with one row per project: path, purpose, activity state, current plan link. Enforce one current plan per project. IDs and records are project-scoped; cross-project references use a qualified form such as `<project-id>:plan-03`. Nested `AGENTS.md` files contain only additions, never a copy of the root guide.

### Document responsibilities

| Document | Owns | Keep out |
|---|---|---|
| README.md | Purpose, layout, how the workspace works, where to start; a pointer to `ROADMAP.md` for the current position | Progress state and history (they drift; `ROADMAP.md` owns them) |
| AGENTS.md | Working agreement, resume routine, planning rules, role-specific protocol, records maintenance | Roadmap, design, transcripts |
| Client entry files (`CLAUDE.md` …) | A pointer to `AGENTS.md`; client-only notes | A copy of `AGENTS.md` |
| ROADMAP.md | Ordered milestones, plan states, resume pointer, gates, provisional estimates | Detailed tasks for future milestones; history |
| MEMORY.md | Decisions, conventions, the time log, references, recent history | A second competing roadmap; invented preferences; long tool recipes |
| History archive (optional) | Older history entries moved out of MEMORY at compaction, one file per month | Decisions or conventions (those stay in MEMORY) |
| Tooling notes (optional) | Tool recipes, API quirks, environment reference material, verified commands | Decisions, progress |
| Domain document(s) | Project-specific concept or design that plans refer to: the *what and why*; with several, a `design/README.md` index (one line per doc) | Progress claims; plan steps |
| Concept glossary (optional) | The project's tool, framework and engine concepts, each explained once and linked from plans; created when the first concept is explained | Progress; decisions; generic programming lessons |
| Current plan | User part first (target, new and also-used line, estimate, tasks, send line), agent notes below the divider; see *Plan format* | Bookkeeping above the divider; steps that rely on an earlier plan |
| Completed plan files | Record of what was planned and delivered | Rewritten history |

Add domain-specific documents only when the actual project needs them. Do not generate empty documents. Optional files omitted from the workspace must also be omitted from navigation links.

## Planning rules

- Maintain a broad roadmap and **one current plan**. Do not write future plans during bootstrap.
- Author the next plan only after the current one has passed review with evidence; the user confirms before it is authored, and an arc's first plan follows the arc review.
- Verify what is verifiable before authoring (environment, filesystem, installed tools).
- A plan ends in an observable, reviewable result; its size fits the work and the user's pace.
- Split a milestone before authoring its plan when: acceptance depends on later milestones · independent systems share only a final proof · several risky unknowns need early checks · no reviewable result appears within each group of work · a first-contact slice (what the next plans immediately depend on) separates cleanly from a completion slice that can wait until those plans need it.
- Design decisions the user may not be able to judge (layout, composition, structure) are drafted by the agent into a spec built from the reference material and corrected by the user; build steps then link that spec so the user judges concrete options instead of inventing.
- Keep plan IDs stable; a split after authoring keeps the number with letter suffixes (`03a`, `03b`), and any divergence between run order and numeric order is stated explicitly (for example under the roadmap table). Completed plan files remain as records.
- Mark finished items (steps, tasks, cards) ✅ when the user reports them done against their **Done when:** (the plan-end review adds fix steps for anything it finds), and update the header grid and next pointer in the same pass; acceptance criteria stay `[ ]` until the plan is Verified, then mark `[x]`.
- Changes to acceptance criteria must be justified and recorded. Never narrow them silently.
- Keep future roadmap entries outcome-level; treat their internals as provisional.
- Label estimates as rough and provisional; never invent delivery dates or commitments.
- Fold the previous plan's recorded learnings into the next plan.

Plan-format rules for every plan (*Plan format* gives the full format):

- Plan content that describes or recreates something visual (a build step, an approach description, a record note) links the reference or generated diagram that shows it (relative path, for example `../refs/<topic>/…`) so the picture sits beside the text.
- The plan header line carries the state, a progress grid (`⬜`/`✅`), the next item and the roadmap link.
- Plans are agent-neutral: they name files, commands and outcomes, not client-specific tool names, so any supported agent client can execute them.
- Each fact has one home: design docs (what/why), plans (how/now), the glossary (concepts), `MEMORY.md` (decisions, history), `ROADMAP.md` (where we are). Other documents link to it (`../design/<doc>.md#<section>`) instead of repeating it.

## Arcs, coverage and time

**Coverage map.** A table in `ROADMAP.md` with one row per topic cluster (a group of related features, not a project): cluster · what it includes · scope (`core` or `later`) · arc · status (`—`, `planned`, or `covered` with links to the plans that covered it). Clusters the user practised before the workspace are listed with the status `before`, so arcs spend their time on what is new. Out-of-scope topics are listed once below the table with where the user learns them instead. A new interest becomes a new row; the agent proposes its scope and the user decides.

**Core and value.** A cluster is `core` when most projects of the kind the user wants to build need it, or when the user's stated target needs it; everything else is `later`. The core is sized so that its estimate fits a period the user agrees is worth spending, stated in the roadmap. Growing the core needs the user's agreement at an arc review.

**Arcs.** The core is covered in arcs of about four or five plans with a common theme, ordered by the user's goal: what the target needs soonest, and what later arcs build on. Each plan introduces one cluster (two at most) and uses earlier ones again with complete steps. Only the current plan is written; the current arc's other plans are one-line outcomes, and later arcs stay one-line themes until they start. Where the track has a distributable build (a packaged game, a deployed app), the arc's last plan or its review produces one.

**Arc review** at the end of every arc, short and with the user: update the coverage map; compare the hours spent with the estimates and re-estimate the remaining core; record new interests as rows; confirm, reorder or drop the next arc; then write its first plan. The user can end the core early at any arc review.

**Session-sized tasks.** Each task fits one of the user's usual sessions and ends at a natural stopping point with something visible, runnable or testable. A plan is a handful of tasks, and its estimate is stated in sessions.

**Self-contained plans.** A plan never depends on the user remembering another plan. Anything built before is written out again in full when a plan needs it, and a plan starts from a clean project, starter or template, not from an earlier plan's files. Shared raw files (sounds, images, data) may be reused by path, with the import steps written out.

**Time.** `ROADMAP.md` carries a time section:

- The budget: sessions per week, session length, and the share of planned sessions that realistically happen (80% until the time log shows otherwise), giving realistic hours per week.
- Per arc: plans, estimated hours as a range, hours spent, and calendar weeks at the realistic weekly hours; a core total with cumulative weeks, so the user can see where stopping early would land.
- Estimates are rough and provisional: plan hours are its sessions times the session length plus about 10% for review fixes; an arc adds an allowance for its review and any arc-end build.
- The time log in `MEMORY.md` records each plan's estimate and actual hours, reported by the user at the plan's end. At each arc review, scale the remaining estimates by the ratio of actual to estimated hours so far, and say so in the roadmap. Never state delivery dates.

## Plan format

```markdown
# Plan NN — [Short title]
`[Planned|Pending|In progress|Done|Verified]` · `⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜ n/N` · next → N.N · arc A · roadmap: ../ROADMAP.md

🎯 [Target — the observable result, one or two lines.]
🆕 New: [the cluster(s) this plan introduces] · Also used: [earlier features this plan uses again, written out in full]
⏱️ Estimate: [n sessions, about h–h hours]

### 1. [Action] · ~1 session
&emsp;&emsp;1.1 [Step: exact path, field values and names; the expected result where it is not obvious]

&emsp;&emsp;1.2 [Step]

💡 How [concept] works here:
- [How it works in this plan, naming the files, assets or steps involved, and why it is built this way.]
- Use it when: [the situations in other projects where this is the tool to reach for.]
- Nearby: [related feature] ([when you would pick it instead]) · [related feature] ([when])

Background: [Concept](../toolbox.md#concept).

**Done when:** [what is true when this task is complete.]

### 2. [Action] · ~1 session
…

📤 When done: [the evidence only the user can provide] and the hours spent.

---
## 🔧 Agent notes
*Bookkeeping and review only — not implementation reading.*
- **Acceptance** (checked at the plan-end review; marked when Verified): [criteria]
- **Known traps**: [short list]
- **Scope guard**: [what this plan deliberately does not include]
- **Environment** verified [date]: [facts the agent checked itself]
- **Review**: [what to inspect at the plan-end review, and the limits of what can be checked]
```

Format rules:

- The user part comes first and carries no bookkeeping; everything after the `---` divider is agent material and can be skipped by the user.
- The user part is target, new and also-used line, estimate, tasks, send line. Plans contain only user actions.
- Tasks are numbered `1`, `2`, …; steps are numbered `1.1`, `1.2`, … under their task, each on its own line indented with `&emsp;&emsp;` (Markdown lists cannot express `1.1`). Each task heading carries its session estimate.
- When the user reports a task done, mark each of its steps ✅ at the start of the step line, before the number (`&emsp;&emsp;✅ 1.1 ...`), append ✅ to the task heading (`### 1. [Action] · ~1 session ✅`), and update the header grid and `next →` in the same pass. Fix steps from the plan-end review are added under the task they belong to, and that task loses its ✅ until they pass.
- Steps are complete every time (see *Step detail*). Explanations are colocated at the step that needs them, never a separate study section before the steps.
- A `💡` tip sits where a new concept or a genuine trap does. Its first bullets say how the concept works in this plan and why it is built this way; then come two fixed bullets: **Use it when** (the situations in other projects where this is the tool to reach for, so the user recognises them later) and **Nearby** (two or three related features this plan does not use, one line each on when one would pick it instead). It ends with `Background:` links to the toolbox. No definitions repeated from the toolbox, no metaphors.
- Each task closes with a `**Done when:**` statement the user can check themselves; the aggregate acceptance list lives in the agent block.
- The send line asks only for evidence the agent cannot produce or inspect itself, plus the hours spent.
- Break it on purpose: where a new concept has a failure that is easy to show, add a short `Try it:` step. The user makes one deliberate change, sees what happens and where it shows, then undoes it. One or two per plan.
- Order steps for live feedback: wire up loading first (references, routes, a running server or watcher), then add content, so every save shows a visible or checkable result. No step leaves the project broken for a later step to fix.
- Everything the user types (code, markup, commands, values) uses only characters on a standard keyboard: `-` not `—`, straight quotes not curly ones, `...` not `…`. Prose may use other characters.
- Every step builds the plan's project or practises one of its features; no steps that exist only for ceremony or bookkeeping.

**Toolbox.** `docs/toolbox.md` is the workspace's concept glossary and the user's index of what exists. Each concept a plan introduces gets one entry, written with the plan: what it is (two or three lines), **Use it when**, **Built in** (links to the plans and tasks that used it), **Nearby** (related features and when to pick each) and **Docs** (a link to the official documentation, checked when written). Later plans link the entry instead of explaining the concept again, and add themselves to **Built in** when they are Verified.

## Step detail

- Every step is complete: exact menu paths and field values; node, class, API or command names; code with its file, anchor and the lines to add, replace or delete; and the expected result after each meaningful step. Detail does not fade with repetition.
- Only trivial actions are written briefly: saving, compiling, switching to a window the plan just named, starting a run the plan has already shown. When unsure whether an action is trivial, write it out.
- Never write a step as a goal that assumes knowledge from an earlier plan ("set up movement like before", "add an interaction system"). Anything built in an earlier plan is written out again in full; the toolbox entry is linked for background.
- Design choices (layout, values, names, structure) are supplied by the plan, ready to type; the user never has to invent them.
- A concept met in an earlier plan gets a one-line reminder and a toolbox link instead of a full explanation; its steps are still complete.
- When a step fails, the reply names the likely cause and the fix directly; a fix that changes the plan is added to it as a fix step.

## Records, states and evidence

Plan states (the fourth state is described under *States*):

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Planned | Roadmap entry only; plan not authored |
| Pending | Plan exists; approval or start pending |
| In progress | Implementation or correction is underway |
| Done | The user reports every task complete; the plan-end review remains |
| Verified | Review passed and applicable observable acceptance has evidence |

- `ROADMAP.md` owns the roadmap, plan states and the resume pointer. `MEMORY.md` owns decisions, conventions, the time log, references and history; history entries are labeled `YYYY-MM-DD-NN` (workspace-wide sequence).
- After meaningful work: update `ROADMAP.md` (states, resume pointer) and `MEMORY.md` (history entry, decisions, learning or skill updates); keep them consistent. No session files.
- On the user's "compact": condense history (recent detailed → older one-liners); never silently remove decisions, evidence labels or learning and skill records. Correct errors by annotation, not silent rewriting.

**Record size budget.** The resume routine reads `ROADMAP.md` and `MEMORY.md` every session, so both must stay readable in one pass:

- `MEMORY.md` targets ≤ ~25 KB. History entries are one line each (label · what happened · outcome, with pointers to plans, decisions or commits); review evidence goes in the plan's agent notes, not the history. When the file exceeds the budget, compact proactively and say so in the history entry; the compaction rules above still apply.
- Conventions are rules, one or two lines each. Tool recipes, API quirks, long environment inventories and engine or tool reference material go in the tooling notes (or the applicable add-on) with a one-line pointer in Conventions.
- Tooling notes list a command only after it has been run in the workspace, with the shell it runs in. When the project starts long-running processes (servers, containers, editors), they open with a **Check first** section: how to see what is already running, what "nothing running" looks like, and how to stop it, free a port or reset state.
- `ROADMAP.md`'s resume block is a few lines: position, current plan, next action, gate. No history; that lives in `MEMORY.md`.
- Long-running workspaces may move older one-line history into `docs/history/YYYY-MM.md` at compaction, leaving one pointer line per archived month in `MEMORY.md`. Archived entries are moved verbatim, never rewritten; decisions, conventions and evidence labels stay in `MEMORY.md`.
- Other documents have soft budgets so no file becomes the one large document: `AGENTS.md` ~10 KB (recipes move to tooling notes), `ROADMAP.md` ~10 KB (outcome-level only), each domain or design doc ~15 KB (split by system and update the index), each plan ~25 KB (complete steps make plans longer than in templates whose detail fades; split with letter suffixes, see *Planning rules*).

Evidence categories, kept separate:

1. **Inspection:** what was read or reviewed and what it supports.
2. **Executed checks:** commands or actions actually run, with context and observed results.
3. **User-reported checks:** what the user says they tested, clearly attributed.
4. **Not checked:** missing environments, omitted scenarios, unresolved findings.

Match the check to the claim: use the cheapest check that settles it (targeted inspection before full runs) and escalate only when the scenario requires it. Distinguish "configured correctly" from "actually works": values visible in a tool's UI are evidenced by user screenshots (user-reported), while heavier runtime or session checks are reserved for claims configuration alone cannot settle (constructed state, runtime wiring, integration, feel). Binary or non-text artifacts need suitable evidence; filenames alone are insufficient. Never equate generated files with working behavior, or a planned check with an executed one.

Visual defects (rendering artifacts, misplaced or missing elements): reproduce before fixing, isolate by toggling the suspect element at runtime, and close only on an executed before/after capture where the tooling allows; "it went away" after an unrelated change is not a closure. Parity checks against a reference (template, earlier version) diff the full property set, not a hand-picked list.

**Verification levels** (optional; recommended once checks can be automated; the plan-end review then names one). The project's tooling notes give the exact commands; engine add-ons give recipes (for Unreal: `UNREAL_TEST_AUTOMATION.md`).

| Level | When | Typical content | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fast** | Every change | Build, static and data validation, lint and format checks, unit tests, headless | minutes |
| **Standard** | Plan-end review (default) | Fast plus functional or integration tests of the behavior, including networked or multi-process checks where the behavior spans processes | ≤ ~15 min |
| **Full** | Plan end where acceptance needs it; milestone gates and demos | Standard plus multi-client or integration runs, performance budgets, visual captures compared with references, packaging; then the user's manual check | ~1 h + user time |

Evidence lines record the level, command, result and artifact path, using the evidence categories above. A planned check is never reported as an executed one.

## States and review protocol

Plans: Planned → Pending → In progress → **Done** (the user reports every task complete; the plan-end review remains) → **Verified**.

- During a plan the user works through the tasks and reports each one done (for example `3 done`). The agent marks it ✅ without a full review, and looks into a task mid-plan only when the user asks or a **Done when:** check fails.
- **Plan-end review:** the user sends the 📤 evidence and the hours spent. The agent inspects the project's files, configuration and structure, runs the non-destructive checks it can (build, tests, lint, editor read-backs where a bridge is set up) and reviews the user's evidence of behaviour. Errors come back as fix steps in the plan, with the fix and a short why; the plan is Verified when they pass.
- At Verified: record the hours in the time log, update the roadmap (state, hours spent, resume block) and the coverage map, add the plan to the **Built in** line of the toolbox entries it used, and add a one-line history entry.
- Review replies lead with the verdict: `✅ Plan NN passes`, or `❌ N.N: <finding> → <correction>`, one or two lines per finding, then `Next:`. The full finding goes in the plan's agent notes, not the reply.
- When the last plan of an arc is Verified, hold the arc review (see *Arcs, coverage and time*) before writing the next plan.

## Decisions, conventions and sources

All three live in `MEMORY.md`.

- **Decisions:** stable IDs scoped to the workspace or project; states Confirmed, Proposed, Deferred, Superseded. One line each: decision, basis, rejected alternatives (a few words on why each lost), revisit trigger, and a pointer to where the full reasoning sits (plan section or history entry). Never silently rewritten; a superseded decision names its successor. Ratify Proposed decisions once the work they govern is underway. The basis lives in the repository (a history entry or a file in the workspace), not only in an external file.
- **Tried and dropped:** an approach abandoned during the work is recorded where it happened (the plan's agent notes or a history entry): what was tried, the evidence that ruled it out, what replaced it. A dead end that shaped a decision is also listed among that decision's rejected alternatives.
- **Conventions:** paths, IDs, naming, markers, evidence labels, repository rules (for example which build artifacts to ignore, and an explicit ignore or attribute decision when a new artifact class first appears), compaction rules, supported agent clients. Fetched third-party material keeps a provenance note beside it (source, date, usage) and stays reference-only.
- **References:** checked sources with dates and versions; unchecked items labeled as to-verify. Research prefers official or primary sources; documentation about a tool is not evidence that the local environment was tested.

## Resume routine, AGENTS.md and client entry files

Resume routine: `docs/ROADMAP.md` (roadmap, states, resume pointer) → `docs/MEMORY.md` (decisions, conventions, the time log, recent history) → the current detailed plan → domain documents when design context matters → tooling notes when tool work is next. State the next action as a plan pointer and continue from the recorded position; do not restart planning.

The generated `AGENTS.md` includes, beyond the items in *AGENTS.md additions*:

1. The working agreement and how the user changes it.
2. The exact resume reading order with paths that exist in this workspace, domain documents named.
3. Planning rules: one current plan, on-demand authoring, verify-before-authoring, review gate before the next plan.
4. Authorization boundaries for risky, external or costly actions; repository delegation if any.
5. Records maintenance, compaction rules and the record size budget.
6. The plan markers legend, and when the agent applies the progress markers (see *Planning rules*).
7. Implementation and documentation roots, repository conventions.
8. The user profile: the default (see *Bootstrap procedure*) plus knowledge and preferences actually supplied.
9. The canonical template file and the add-ons used, as references only; the rule to ask the user when a path is missing; the rule to propose template updates when formats change.

Do not copy the template into `AGENTS.md`. Do not insert a technology stack, fixed milestone count, domain-specific verification matrix or experience profile unless the user's requirements justify it.

**Client entry files.** `AGENTS.md` is the single source of agent rules. A client that does not read `AGENTS.md` natively gets a thin entry file that points to it, never a copy. For Claude Code: a root `CLAUDE.md` whose content is `@AGENTS.md` (the import loads the file), plus client-only notes when there are any. Create entry files only for clients the user actually uses, and record the supported clients in `MEMORY.md` conventions. Tool-server (MCP) configuration is per client and per project (for example OpenCode `opencode.json`, Claude Code `.mcp.json`); when more than one client is supported, keep their entries equivalent. The add-ons give the shapes.

## AGENTS.md additions

The generated `AGENTS.md` also includes:

1. How authorized implementation requests change the working agreement.
2. The plan scope rule, with the track's out-of-scope topics and where the user learns them.
3. Step detail: complete steps every time, the trivial-action exception, no reliance on earlier plans.
4. Arcs, coverage and time: the coverage map, the arc review, session-sized tasks, the time section and the time log.
5. The review protocol, evidence categories and the review reply format, plus the bookkeeping done when the user reports a task (steps marked ✅ at the start of their lines, ✅ appended to the task heading, the header grid and `next →` updated) and at Verified (time log, roadmap, coverage map, toolbox, history).
6. The plan markers legend: states Planned → Pending → In progress → Done → Verified; `🎯 🆕 ⏱️ 💡 ✅ ⬜ 📤 🔧`; `**Done when:**` checkpoints; `Try it:` experiments.

## Final audit and handoff

Before reporting the workspace ready, check (plus *Audit additions*):

- All supplied requirements are captured without adding unrequested scope; proposals, observations and open questions are distinguishable.
- Single-project versus multi-project structure is coherent and documented.
- Every active project has at most one current plan; completed plans remain intact; future milestones stay outcome-level.
- Completed items are ✅; acceptance is `[x]` only for Verified plans; states agree with `ROADMAP.md`.
- Records live only in `ROADMAP.md` and `MEMORY.md` (plus optional tooling notes and history archive); no stray status, session or duplicate documents; records and documents are within their size budgets.
- The README holds no progress state; the roadmap's resume block is current.
- The environment the agent can verify was verified before authoring plans.
- Links resolve, tables and fences are valid, and actionable documents have no unresolved boilerplate.
- Evidence labels are honest: only checks actually performed; missing evidence is identified.
- Decisions carry their rejected alternatives and a pointer to the full reasoning; dead ends are recorded where they happened.
- The generated `AGENTS.md` is concise, uses correct paths and agrees with the working role; client entry files point to it.
- Needed add-ons are in use or their absence is recorded.
- The next action is concrete and feasible, or the exact missing prerequisite is identified.

Finish with links to the workspace entry point, roadmap and current plan; state what was created or adapted, what was verified and what remains pending. Do not claim the deliverable is implemented or verified because its documentation has been generated.

## Audit additions

- The current plan is one coherent slice; the next plan is gated on the plan-end review and the user's confirmation, and an arc's first plan on the arc review.
- Plans follow the format: target, new and also-used line, estimate, tasks with session estimates, send line, agent notes below the divider; plans contain only user actions.
- Every step is complete, no step relies on an earlier plan, and only trivial actions are brief.
- Each concept the current plan introduces has a toolbox entry with Use it when, Built in, Nearby and Docs; its tips carry the Use it when and Nearby bullets.
- The roadmap has the time section (budget, realistic share, per-arc estimates and hours spent, core total with cumulative weeks) and a coverage map consistent with the arcs; out-of-scope topics are listed with where the user learns them.
- No skill ledger or support levels appear in the workspace.

## Optional add-ons

Add-ons are separate files in the template repository for specific tooling. They supplement this template and never change its working agreement. Use one when the project involves its area; record the ones used in `MEMORY.md` references.

| Add-on | Use when | If needed but not provided |
|---|---|---|
| `UNREAL_MCP_BRIDGE.md` | An Unreal Engine project where the agent should inspect or edit the editor (MCP bridges, reference-material pipeline) | Ask for it; without it, editor work becomes user steps with screenshot evidence |
| `UNREAL_TEST_AUTOMATION.md` | An Unreal Engine project with automated checks (builds, automation and functional tests, captures, packaging per verification level) | Ask for it; without it, define the commands in the tooling notes as they are verified |
| `BLENDER_MCP_BRIDGE.md` | Blender scene work or batch asset pipelines, Unreal export conventions | Ask for it; without it, Blender work becomes user steps |
| `ASSET_GENERATION_PIPELINE.md` | 3D assets or concept and reference images are sourced or generated (packs, AI 3D, Blender; provenance and licences) | Ask for it; without it, record sources and licences by hand |
| `AGENT_ORCHESTRATION.md` | The autonomous template with a cheaper worker client (dispatch, report format, dry run) | The orchestrator implements the cards itself |

Helper scripts used by the add-ons live in the template repository's `scripts/` folder.
